1	# TAC-5 · Close the Loops — Master Teaching Notes
2	
3	> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 53:52 · Intermediate · Tactic #5: **Always Add Feedback Loops**
4	> Lesson artifact: the tac-5 codebase — a real NL→SQL app (FastAPI + Vite/TS) wrapped in a full agentic layer: 21 command templates (incl. `/test`, `/test_e2e`, 3 e2e specs, 2 resolvers), Playwright MCP, five ADW scripts, and the 1,106-line `adw_test.py` test node.
5	> Subtitle: "More Compute, More Confidence" (course page; the in-video slide footer says "Higher Confidence").
6	
7	**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** Your work is useless until it's validated, so encode how you would test every class of work into commands and tool calls, attach those validators to every agentic prompt (request → validate → resolve), and stack them — linter to unit tests to builds to browser-driving e2e — until agents execute, validate, and resolve in loops and 'the code writes itself,' first in-loop where you can watch, then out-loop where you can't.
8	
9	**The chapter must land ten ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## Idea 1 — The most valuable thing you make is not code, and the question that follows
14	
15	**Hook.** Lesson 5 opens with a confession demand: "Let's be brutally honest with ourselves." Engineers rank code, architecture, systems, plans, features as their most valuable assets — and they're wrong. The valuable thing is the *experience in your users' hands*, which means the highest-value engineering act is proving the stuff does what it's meant to do. Then the ambush: you probably verify by opening the browser and clicking around. "What a waste of time."
16	
17	**Picture.** Frame t0105 (1:45): the two-line question slide — "Given a unit of **valuable work** that's production ready / How would you, the engineer, **test and validate this work?**" This is the lesson's load-bearing artifact; everything else is answers to it.
18	
19	**Worked example.** The lesson's own answer menu (2:28–3:00, narrated over an on-screen checklist): run your linter, execute unit tests, UI tests, CI/CD integration tests, build/compile, look for Datadog log lines, check Sentry for the *absence* of errors, run custom evals or LLM-as-a-judge for ML work — and the big one, clicking through the feature yourself. Every item is a feedback loop, and every one of them is encodable as a command or tool call. In tac-5 those encodings literally exist as files: `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run pytest`, `bun tsc --noEmit`, `bun run build`, `.claude/commands/e2e/*.md`.
20	
21	**Dan's term.** *The core validation question.* And the payoff clause: answer it "for every class of work that your codebase handles and then encode the answers into a command or tool call, [and] you will fly while other engineers run." Plus the architecture rider: *codebase architecture is a massive critical leverage point* here — "net new codebases have a massive advantage."
22	
23	**Failure mode.** Treating the question as rhetorical instead of operational. The deliverable is a literal list: per class of work, the exact commands that would prove it production-ready. If you can't write the command, you haven't answered the question — and your agent has no loop to close. (Lab S5 makes students produce this list for their own repo.)
24	
25	**Retrieval Q.** Recite the core validation question and state what you do with the answer. *(Given a unit of valuable work that's production ready, how would you, the engineer, test and validate this work? — answer it per class of work, encode each answer into a command or tool call.)*
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Idea 2 — Tactic #5: Always Add Feedback Loops (the testing debate is over)
30	
31	**Hook.** One of engineering's most heated debates — how much testing is worth it — "has come to an end." Not by argument, by arithmetic: the value of a test used to amortize over *your* runs of it; now it multiplies by the number of *agent executions* in your codebase, and that number is exploding.
32	
33	**Picture.** Frame t0230 (3:50): the official Tactic card — "Always Add Feedback Loops" with the Daily Actions sidebar: add validation commands to every agentic prompt; create closed-loop prompts (request, validate, resolve); set up e2e tests for high-ROI self-validation; chain feedback mechanisms; spend compute on testing to buy confidence in agent work.
34	
35	**Worked example.** The lesson's KPI logic (7:28, recap of the TAC-2 scoreboard): attempts down, size up, streak up, presence down. Every one moves the right way when agents self-validate: fewer re-prompts (attempts), bigger units of handed-off work (size), more consecutive one-shots (streak), fewer moments where you must be present (presence). Testing is "one of the highest through-agent leverage points" because it converts compute into confidence without you.
36	
37	**Dan's term.** *Always add feedback loops* — with both halves said explicitly: "I'm not saying stop testing or stop reviewing. I'm saying start handing off this responsibility and start teaching your agents to test." The hierarchy: "The ultimate test will always be your users. The next best test... used to be you. Now, the next best test is an army of agents validating your entire codebase with regression tests and most importantly with end-to-end tests." And the verdict: "engineers that test with their agents win. Full stop, zero exceptions."
38	
39	**Failure mode.** Hearing 'add feedback loops' as a someday-testing-strategy instead of a *prompt-structure rule for today*. The test of the tactic is brutal and immediate: does the prompt you are about to fire contain a validation block? If not, you just volunteered to be the validator — the exact job the lesson exists to hand off. Second failure: judging test ROI with human-era math ("tests slow me down"), which silently converts every agent run from self-validating to unverified.
40	
41	**Retrieval Q.** Why is the testing debate over, and what are the two things the tactic does NOT mean? *(Test value multiplies by agent executions, so engineers who test with agents win — full stop; it doesn't mean stop testing/reviewing yourself entirely, and it doesn't mean 'later' — it means every agentic prompt carries validators now.)*
42	
43	---
44	
45	## Idea 3 — Three loops that sound alike: in-loop, out-loop, closing the loop
46	
47	**Hook.** Three phrases, one word apart, and mixing them up costs you the lesson: being *in* the loop, being *out* of the loop, and *closing* the loop. You can be out-loop with zero closed loops — that's an unsupervised agent shipping unverified junk. The lesson's whole strategy is: close the loops in-loop where you can watch, so you can trust them out-loop where you can't.
48	
49	**Picture.** No slide exists (spoken over B-roll, 4:54–5:30) — the chapter should draw the three-loop diagram: (1) you ↔ agent chat cycle (in-loop), (2) the PITER pipeline running on a separate machine (out-loop), (3) the micro-loop inside any single step: agent → command → feedback → agent (closing the loop). Frames t0700/t0725 (11:40/12:05) supply the out-loop half in the real world: the GitHub issue whose body is `adw_plan_build_test` + `/feature` + a mid-level prompt, and the Mac mini running `trigger_webhook.py` that catches it.
50	
51	**Worked example.** The lesson performs all three simultaneously: at 10:13 Dan fires the out-loop pipeline (issue #28 → webhook → plan→build→test on the agent box), then spends thirty minutes in-loop demonstrating the closed-loop primitives that pipeline is built from, then returns at 46:32 to find a PR waiting. The demo's structure IS the concept.
52	
53	**Dan's term.** *In-loop* ("you sitting right here, prompting with your agent back and forth"), *out-loop* ("a high level prompt running through the PITER system that fires off on your isolated device" — PITER from TAC-4: Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review; the transcript's 'Peter system' and 'PIDA framework' are mishearings), and *closing the loop*: "letting your agent operate on work, calling a command or a tool to get feedback on the success of the work... your agent continues to build until the feedback is positive. When you do this, you let the code write itself."
54	
55	**Failure mode.** Conflating out-loop with closed-loop and scaling autonomy before feedback: firing AFK agents on a codebase with no validators. Autonomy without feedback is unsupervised risk; feedback is what makes autonomy safe to scale. Reverse failure: staying in-loop forever polishing validators and never installing a trigger + environment — the KPI gains (presence↓, size↑) only materialize out-loop.
56	
57	**Retrieval Q.** Define the three terms so they can't be confused. *(In-loop: you at the keyboard trading prompts. Out-loop: a high-level prompt running via PITER on an isolated machine. Closing the loop: the agent calling commands/tools for feedback on its own work and iterating until positive.)*
58	
59	---
60	
61	## Idea 4 — The closed-loop prompt: Request → Validate → Resolve
62	
63	**Hook.** The lesson's first artifact is three lines long, and one of the lines is an order to sabotage the codebase. That's the point: the prompt plants a defect *and* carries the loop that catches it. If a three-line prompt can self-correct, "I don't have time for feedback loops" is dead on arrival.
64	
65	**Picture.** Frame t0860 (14:20): the scratch buffer, verbatim — `Update @app/server/core/sql_processor.py comment out validation.` / `Validate your work with `cd app/server && uv run ruff check .``. If there are errors at all, resolve them.` Frame t0985 (16:25): the next-level version actually closing — ruff's E402 in the terminal, and the agent's own sentence: "I need to fix the ruff errors. The issue is that load_dotenv() is being called before all imports are complete. I need to move it after all the imports."
66

77	## Idea 5 — Stack the loops; make tests the rule of law

79	**Hook.** The best moment of the lesson is a trap paying off: demo 1 deliberately left a landmine (validation commented out), and demo 2 — run by a *fresh agent with a cleared context window* — steps on it. Pytest fails, and an agent that never saw the sabotage un-comments the line and restores the import. Nobody remembered the defect. The validator did.
80	
81	**Picture.** Frame t1030 (17:10): the diff restoring `validate_sql_query(sql_query)` and the `SQLSecurityError` import, with "Now let's run pytest again" beneath — the cross-context catch on camera.
82	
83	**Worked example.** Demo 2 (15:15–17:40): request = remove the `/api/insights` endpoint from `server.py`, move `load_dotenv()` right below its import; validate = ruff, `uv run pytest`, `uv run python -m py_compile server.py`; resolve = fix everything found. Ruff catches the E402 import-order issue; the agent briefly adds duplicate imports ("This happens.") and re-runs; pytest catches demo 1's sabotage "without knowing what we previously did, thanks to the context window clearing"; py_compile seals syntax. Three loops, each covering a failure class the others can't see. What's more important, the code or your tests? The answer should be your tests. **Your tests should be the rule of law in your codebase.**" With the corollary: if the tests aren't right, have your agents update the *tests* so testing commands keep their weight. And the forward-looking reason: "as the agents progress, as the models improve, **we will be the ones prompting the errors**" — loops guard against your prompts, not just the model's slips.

87	**Failure mode.** Two. (a) Stopping at one validator: the linter can't catch a failing business rule; nothing but an e2e run catches 'the button doesn't work.' Confidence is coverage of *disjoint failure classes*. (b) The rule-of-law inversion: letting an agent (or yourself) weaken a red test to get to green. The moment a failing validator is negotiable, every loop in the repo stops meaning anything — feedback becomes advisory, and self-validation quietly dies.
88	
89	**Retrieval Q.** Name the six loops of the lesson and state the rule of law with its corollary. *(ruff, pytest, py_compile, tsc --noEmit, bun run build, Playwright e2e; tests outrank code — red means stop and fix, and a wrong test gets visibly fixed as a test, never routed around.)*

# TAC-5 · Close the Loops — Master Teaching Notes

> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 53:52 · Intermediate · Tactic #5: **Always Add Feedback Loops**
> Lesson artifact: the tac-5 codebase — a real NL→SQL app (FastAPI + Vite/TS) wrapped in a full agentic layer: 21 command templates (incl. `/test`, `/test_e2e`, 3 e2e specs, 2 resolvers), Playwright MCP, five ADW scripts, and the 1,106-line `adw_test.py` test node.
> Subtitle: "More Compute, More Confidence" (course page; the in-video slide footer says "Higher Confidence").

**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** Your work is useless until it's validated, so encode how you would test every class of work into commands and tool calls, attach those validators to every agentic prompt (request → validate → resolve), and stack them — linter to unit tests to builds to browser-driving e2e — until agents execute, validate, and resolve in loops and 'the code writes itself,' first in-loop where you can watch, then out-loop where you can't.

**The chapter must land ten ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.

---

## Idea 1 — The most valuable thing you make is not code, and the question that follows

**Hook.** Lesson 5 opens with a confession demand: "Let's be brutally honest with ourselves." Engineers rank code, architecture, systems, plans, features as their most valuable assets — and they're wrong. The valuable thing is the *experience in your users' hands*, which means the highest-value engineering act is proving the stuff does what it's meant to do. Then the ambush: you probably verify by opening the browser and clicking around. "What a waste of time."

**Picture.** Frame t0105 (1:45): the two-line question slide — "Given a unit of **valuable work** that's production ready / How would you, the engineer, **test and validate this work?**" This is the lesson's load-bearing artifact; everything else is answers to it.

**Worked example.** The lesson's own answer menu (2:28–3:00, narrated over an on-screen checklist): run your linter, execute unit tests, UI tests, CI/CD integration tests, build/compile, look for Datadog log lines, check Sentry for the *absence* of errors, run custom evals or LLM-as-a-judge for ML work — and the big one, clicking through the feature yourself. Every item is a feedback loop, and every one of them is encodable as a command or tool call. In tac-5 those encodings literally exist as files: `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run pytest`, `bun tsc --noEmit`, `bun run build`, `.claude/commands/e2e/*.md`.

**Dan's term.** *The core validation question.* And the payoff clause: answer it "for every class of work that your codebase handles and then encode the answers into a command or tool call, [and] you will fly while other engineers run." Plus the architecture rider: *codebase architecture is a massive critical leverage point* here — "net new codebases have a massive advantage."

**Failure mode.** Treating the question as rhetorical instead of operational. The deliverable is a literal list: per class of work, the exact commands that would prove it production-ready. If you can't write the command, you haven't answered the question — and your agent has no loop to close. (Lab S5 makes students produce this list for their own repo.)

## Idea 2 — Tactic #5: Always Add Feedback Loops (the testing debate is over)

**Hook.** One of engineering's most heated debates — how much testing is worth it — "has come to an end." Not by argument, by arithmetic: the value of a test used to amortize over *your* runs of it; now it multiplies by the number of *agent executions* in your codebase, and that number is exploding.

**Picture.** Frame t0230 (3:50): the official Tactic card — "Always Add Feedback Loops" with the Daily Actions sidebar: add validation commands to every agentic prompt; create closed-loop prompts (request, validate, resolve); set up e2e tests for high-ROI self-validation; chain feedback mechanisms; spend compute on testing to buy confidence in agent work.

**Worked example.** The lesson's KPI logic (7:28, recap of the TAC-2 scoreboard): attempts down, size up, streak up, presence down. Every one moves the right way when agents self-validate: fewer re-prompts (attempts), bigger units of handed-off work (size), more consecutive one-shots (streak), fewer moments where you must be present (presence). Testing is "one of the highest through-agent leverage points" because it converts compute into confidence without you.

**Dan's term.** *Always add feedback loops* — with both halves said explicitly: "I'm not saying stop testing or stop reviewing. Now, the next best test is an army of agents validating your entire codebase with regression tests and most importantly with end-to-end tests." And the verdict: "engineers that test with their agents win. Full stop, zero exceptions."

The test of the tactic is brutal and immediate: does the prompt you are about to fire contain a validation block? If not, you just volunteered to be the validator — the exact job the lesson exists to hand off. Second failure: judging test ROI with human-era math ("tests slow me down"), which silently converts every agent run from self-validating to unverified.

## Idea 3 — Three loops that sound alike: in-loop, out-loop, closing the loop

**Hook.** Three phrases, one word apart, and mixing them up costs you the lesson: being *in* the loop, being *out* of the loop, and *closing* the loop. You can be out-loop with zero closed loops — that's an unsupervised agent shipping unverified junk. The lesson's whole strategy is: close the loops in-loop where you can watch, so you can trust them out-loop where you can't.

**Picture.** No slide exists (spoken over B-roll, 4:54–5:30) — the chapter should draw the three-loop diagram: (1) you ↔ agent chat cycle (in-loop), (2) the PITER pipeline running on a separate machine (out-loop), (3) the micro-loop inside any single step: agent → command → feedback → agent (closing the loop). Frames t0700/t0725 (11:40/12:05) supply the out-loop half in the real world: the GitHub issue whose body is `adw_plan_build_test` + `/feature` + a mid-level prompt, and the Mac mini running `trigger_webhook.py` that catches it.

**Worked example.** The lesson performs all three simultaneously: at 10:13 Dan fires the out-loop pipeline (issue #28 → webhook → plan→build→test on the agent box), then spends thirty minutes in-loop demonstrating the closed-loop primitives that pipeline is built from, then returns at 46:32 to find a PR waiting. The demo's structure IS the concept.

**Dan's term.** *In-loop* ("you sitting right here, prompting with your agent back and forth"), *out-loop* ("a high level prompt running through the PITER system that fires off on your isolated device" — PITER from TAC-4: Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review; the transcript's 'Peter system' and 'PIDA framework' are mishearings), and *closing the loop*: "letting your agent operate on work, calling a command or a tool to get feedback on the success of the work... your agent continues to build until the feedback is positive. When you do this, you let the code write itself."

**Failure mode.** Conflating out-loop with closed-loop and scaling autonomy before feedback: firing AFK agents on a codebase with no validators. Autonomy without feedback is unsupervised risk; feedback is what makes autonomy safe to scale. Reverse failure: staying in-loop forever polishing validators and never installing a trigger + environment — the KPI gains (presence↓, size↑) only materialize out-loop.

**Retrieval Q.** Define the three terms so they can't be confused. *(In-loop: you at the keyboard trading prompts. Out-loop: a high-level prompt running via PITER on an isolated machine. Closing the loop: the agent calling commands/tools for feedback on its own work and iterating until positive.)*

## Idea 4 — The closed-loop prompt: Request → Validate → Resolve

**Hook.** The lesson's first artifact is three lines long, and one of the lines is an order to sabotage the codebase. That's the point: the prompt plants a defect *and* carries the loop that catches it. If a three-line prompt can self-correct, "I don't have time for feedback loops" is dead on arrival.

**Picture.** Frame t0860 (14:20): the scratch buffer, verbatim — `Update @app/server/core/sql_processor.py comment out validation.` / `Validate your work with `cd app/server && uv run ruff check .``. If there are errors at all, resolve them.` Frame t0985 (16:25): the next-level version actually closing — ruff's E402 in the terminal, and the agent's own sentence: "I need to fix the ruff errors. The issue is that load_dotenv() is being called before all imports are complete. I need to move it after all the imports."

**Worked example.** Demo 1 (13:38–14:50): commenting out `validate_sql_query(sql_query)` in `core/sql_processor.py` leaves its import dangling; `uv run ruff check .` prints the unused-import error to stdout; that stdout lands in the agent's context window; the agent fixes and reruns ruff to green. "Ruff is looking at that change. It's going to provide input back to our agent via standard out." The feedback channel is embarrassingly ordinary — and that's why it works everywhere: *everything is one tool call away; tools are just functions and functions can do anything* (9:49).

**Dan's term.** *Closed loop prompt*, with its *anatomy*: "There's a request — usually a large spec or task or feature you want built — and then you're going to have validations... validators, and then give some direction with your resolution. Request, validate, resolve." Plus the execution rule from the scaled version: run validators in order, top to bottom; on any issue, stop, resolve immediately, then "rerun every validation step. It's not good enough to resolve this once and [have] that resolution cause something to break."

**Failure mode.** Writing the request and skipping the validation block because the change is 'simple.' An open-loop prompt doesn't fail loudly — it silently reassigns the validator job to you, later, when you least expect it. Second failure: believing the magic is in the model. The magic is in the plumbing: no validator in the prompt → no stdout in context → no self-correction, however smart the agent.

**Retrieval Q.** Write the lesson's smallest closed-loop prompt from memory and name its three parts. *(Request: comment out validation in sql_processor.py. Validate: cd app/server && uv run ruff check . Resolve: if there are errors at all, resolve them.)*

## Idea 5 — Stack the loops; make tests the rule of law

**Hook.** The best moment of the lesson is a trap paying off: demo 1 deliberately left a landmine (validation commented out), and demo 2 — run by a *fresh agent with a cleared context window* — steps on it. Pytest fails, and an agent that never saw the sabotage un-comments the line and restores the import. Nobody remembered the defect. The validator did.

**Picture.** Frame t1030 (17:10): the diff restoring `validate_sql_query(sql_query)` and the `SQLSecurityError` import, with "Now let's run pytest again" beneath — the cross-context catch on camera.

**Worked example.** Demo 2 (15:15–17:40): request = remove the `/api/insights` endpoint from `server.py`, move `load_dotenv()` right below its import; validate = ruff, `uv run pytest`, `uv run python -m py_compile server.py`; resolve = fix everything found. Ruff catches the E402 import-order issue; the agent briefly adds duplicate imports ("This happens.") and re-runs; pytest catches demo 1's sabotage "without knowing what we previously did, thanks to the context window clearing"; py_compile seals syntax. Three loops, each covering a failure class the others can't see. By 25:20 the full stack counts six: ruff, pytest ("a crap ton more than one, but one bucket"), py_compile, `bun tsc --noEmit`, `bun run build`, Playwright e2e.

**Dan's term.** *Stacking the confidence* ("We know a little bit more, a little bit better that things are going to work") and the architecture decree: "You have to make a rule inside of your codebase architecture. What's more important, the code or your tests? The answer should be your tests. **Your tests should be the rule of law in your codebase.**" With the corollary: if the tests aren't right, have your agents update the *tests* so testing commands keep their weight. And the forward-looking reason: "as the agents progress, as the models improve, **we will be the ones prompting the errors**" — loops guard against your prompts, not just the model's slips.

**Failure mode.** Two. (a) Stopping at one validator: the linter can't catch a failing business rule; nothing but an e2e run catches 'the button doesn't work.' Confidence is coverage of *disjoint failure classes*. (b) The rule-of-law inversion: letting an agent (or yourself) weaken a red test to get to green. The moment a failing validator is negotiable, every loop in the repo stops meaning anything — feedback becomes advisory, and self-validation quietly dies.

**Retrieval Q.** Name the six loops of the lesson and state the rule of law with its corollary. *(ruff, pytest, py_compile, tsc --noEmit, bun run build, Playwright e2e; tests outrank code — red means stop and fix, and a wrong test gets visibly fixed as a test, never routed around.)*

## Idea 7 — Template your engineering: validation by default

**Hook.** "Always add feedback loops" has an enemy: your discipline on a busy Tuesday. The lesson's answer is to take 'always' away from the human entirely — bake the loops into the templates that generate all future work, so forgetting is no longer an available action.

**Picture.** Frame t1760 (29:20): `bug.md`'s Plan Format — the `## Validation Commands` block ("Execute every command to validate the bug is fixed with zero regressions"), the reproduce-before/after placeholder, the three default commands (`uv run pytest`, `bun tsc --noEmit`, `bun run build`), and the conditional e2e machinery. Frame t0700 (11:40) shows where these plans come from out-loop: the issue body itself.

**Worked example.** `/bug` is a *meta prompt* — "a prompt that creates a prompt": (issue_number, adw_id, issue_json) → a plan in `specs/issue-{n}-adw-{id}-sdlc_planner-{slug}.md`. Fired in-loop on camera: `/bug 111 adw111` for the junk-data bug (tests writing to the production SQLite DB — "our tests shouldn't be operating in our quote-unquote live production database"; fix: in-memory DBs). The generated plan arrives with reproduce steps, root-cause analysis, and validation commands (sqlite3 table checks, targeted pytest, before/after table diffs) — and correctly *omits* an e2e task because the bug is backend-only: the template's "IMPORTANT: If the bug affects the UI or user interactions..." conditional didn't fire. A second agent runs `/bug 222 adw222` (disable query input while running + debounce — "a common UI thing... not something that you or I need to solve ever again"), whose plan DOES include creating `.claude/commands/e2e/test_<name>.md`. Then `/implement <plan>` (a higher-order prompt whose `think hard` is an information-dense keyword activating extended thinking) executes plan 111, finishing with its validation commands. "Plan velocity is through the roof... Great planning is indeed great prompting."

**Dan's term.** *Templating our engineering* — "you encode it, you template your engineering into your reusable prompts so that your agents can pick up on the work and build the way you want to build over and over and over. And the way you want to build is with high confidence." Also *fresh agents*: "/clear... we always want fresh agent instances. We don't want any context pollution" — plus the in-loop constraint noted on camera: one repo-mutating agent at a time on your device (no worktrees in this lesson), a limitation the out-loop architecture removes.

**Failure mode.** Hand-adding validation commands to individual prompts and calling it a system — hand-added loops disappear the week you're busy; templated loops are structural. Subtler failure: not auditing the conditional — a UI bug whose plan lacks an e2e task means the template misfired, and rubber-stamping it erodes the guarantee the template exists to provide.

**Retrieval Q.** What does the /bug meta prompt guarantee about every plan it generates, and when does it force a new e2e test file? *(Every plan ends with a Validation Commands section — pytest/tsc/build defaults plus reproduce-before/after commands; a new .claude/commands/e2e/test_<name>.md task is forced whenever the bug affects UI or user interactions.)*

## Idea 8 — adw_test: the test step becomes an isolated ADW node

**Hook.** Everything so far ran where you could watch it. The last move is packaging the whole testing discipline into a machine you *don't* watch: a script that runs every test you have, tries to fix what fails, reports everything, and ships its results — as its own node of the SDLC, separate from plan and build.

**Picture.** Frame t2460 (41:00): `adw_test.py`'s `run_tests_with_resolution` — `max_attempts: int = MAX_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS`, `while attempt < max_attempts:`, the circled `run_tests(adw_id, logger)` — deterministic Python wrapped around agentic judgment, with the `adws/` module tree and the freshly-generated issue-111/222 specs in the explorer.

**Worked example.** The pipeline, verified against the 1,106-line source: fetch issue → checkout the state branch (or create `test-issue-{n}-adw-{id}`) → `/test` runs the five-check suite and must return ONLY a JSON array of `{test_name, passed, execution_command, test_purpose, error?}`, failures first ("we'll immediately run JSON.parse() on the output") → each failure fans out to a fresh `/resolve_failed_test` agent (`test_resolver_iter{attempt}_{idx}`) that must *reproduce via the provided execution_command* before fixing, minimally, and re-run only that command → up to `MAX_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 4` rounds, stopping early if a round resolves nothing → e2e gate: only if unit tests are green and `--skip-e2e` absent → glob `.claude/commands/e2e/*.md`, run each via `/test_e2e` (agents `e2e_test_runner_{attempt-1}_{idx}`), **stop at the first e2e failure**, resolve via `/resolve_failed_e2e_test`, `MAX_E2E_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 2` → post the 📊 Test Run Summary to the issue → `/commit` → push + create/update PR → exit 1 if failures remain. "What do you think the failed tests do? Of course, they do one thing. They run a template."

**Dan's term.** *AI Developer Workflow* (the highest leverage point, "the highest composition level"), *isolated nodes*: "It's isolated. It's not part of the build. It's not part of the plan. This runs on its own with its own set of agents in its own context windows... we want to be able to tap into one node of the software developer lifecycle and improve that one node." Plus the composition move: `adw_plan_build_test.py` subprocesses plan → build → test sharing one ADW ID and `agents/{id}/adw_state.json` — "isolated reusable scripts" via astral uv ("you can use anything you want — classic shell scripts, bun scripts").

**Failure mode.** Wiring test-running into the build agent 'to keep it simple' — you lose all three isolations at once: fresh context per failure, an independently improvable node, and the JSON boundary where *code* (not vibes) decides what happens next. Second failure: reading the retry constants as arbitrary. Bounded loops (4/2, stop-on-nothing-resolved, e2e-stop-on-first-failure) are what separate a self-correcting system from a token-burning one that thrashes on an unfixable failure.

**Retrieval Q.** Walk adw_test.py's control flow with its bounds. *(/test → JSON parse → per-failure resolver agents, ≤4 rounds, early-stop if nothing resolved; e2e only on green units and no --skip-e2e: per-file /test_e2e, stop at first failure, /resolve_failed_e2e_test, ≤2 rounds; summary → commit → push/PR; non-zero exit on remaining failures.)*

## Terminology glossary (Dan-isms, canonical spellings)

- **Tactic #5: Always Add Feedback Loops** — every agentic prompt carries validators
- **The core validation question** — "Given a unit of valuable work that's production ready, how would you, the engineer, test and validate this work?"
- **Closed loop prompt** — request → validate → resolve; the agent tests itself
- **Closing the loop** — agent calls a command/tool for feedback and iterates until positive; "let the code write itself"
- **In-loop / out-loop** — you at the keyboard vs. a PITER-driven pipeline on an isolated machine
- **PITER** — Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review (TAC-4; mishearings: 'Peter system', 'PIDA framework')
- **Rule of law** — tests outrank code; wrong tests get fixed as tests
- **Stacking the confidence** — adding validators across disjoint failure classes (six in this lesson)
- **Meta prompt** — a prompt that creates a prompt (/bug, /feature, /chore → plans)
- **Higher order prompt (HOP)** — a prompt taking another prompt/file as argument (/implement, /test_e2e)
- **Information dense keyword (IDK)** — special-effect words, e.g. `think hard` (extended thinking)

# TAC-5 Lab Spec — Close the Loops

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → the tac-5 NL→SQL app; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-5.git`, then re-origin to your OWN GitHub repo so you control the issues/PRs the out-loop drills create). No external repos.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. Every mutation flows through a prompt — scratch-buffer prompt files are allowed and encouraged; opening the editor to "just fix it" is a failed lab.
**Second directive:** every prompt you fire carries a validation block. A request without a `validate` section is you volunteering to be the validator — the exact job this lesson exists to hand off.
**Time box:** 90–150 minutes (53:52 lesson, six reproduce drills + five stretch). Token cost: a long lesson of real agent runs — several in-loop closed loops plus at least one full `adw_test.py` node (plan/test/e2e agents). Pay to play; budget for it.

---

## 0 · Setup (15 min)

1. Clone and take ownership: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-5.git && cd tac-5`, create your own GitHub repo, `git remote set-url origin <yours>` (you need issues/PRs you control).
2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `bun --version`, `gh auth status`. Playwright MCP deps resolve on first use via `.mcp.json` (`npx @playwright/mcp@latest`).
3. Configure env: `cp .env.sample .env` (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` required for programmatic Claude Code) and `cp app/server/.env.sample app/server/.env` (OpenAI and/or Anthropic key for the NL→SQL feature).
4. **Permissions & control audit (do not skip):** open `.claude/settings.json` and answer in writing — name the deny rules (e.g. `git push --force`, `rm -rf`) and the five lifecycle hook events. Then read `.claude/commands/install.md` **before** you run it. Dan's rule: *"always review these slash commands... they have massive control."*
5. Boot: run `/install` in Claude Code (or manually: `uv sync --all-extras` in `app/server`, `bun install` in `app/client`, `sh scripts/reset_db.sh`, `sh scripts/start.sh`). Confirm `http://localhost:5173` renders with the sample tables. If the port is taken, use the stop/start scripts (Dan hits this on camera).

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, what the agent may NOT do (deny rules) and which slash commands can mutate your repo. If you can't, re-read the files — reviewing the agentic layer before running it is a graded habit.

## 1 · The simplest closed loop (10 min)

In a scratch markdown buffer write the three-part prompt **exactly**:
- **Request:** comment out validation in `@app/server/core/sql_processor.py`
- **Validate:** `` cd app/server && uv run ruff check . ``
- **Resolve:** "If there are errors at all, resolve them."

Fire it. Watch ruff's stdout enter the agent's context window (the unused-import error from the now-dangling import), then watch the agent fix it and re-run ruff to green. Verify independently: `uv run ruff check .` → clean.

**Checkpoint 1:** name the three parts of what you just fired, and name the feedback channel. *(Request / Validate / Resolve; the channel is ordinary stdout landing in the context window — "everything is one tool call away.")*

## 2 · Three loops + the sabotage catch (15 min)

**`/clear` FIRST — this is the entire point of the drill.** New prompt: remove the `/api/insights` endpoint from `@app/server/server.py` and move `load_dotenv()` right below its import; validate with ruff, `uv run pytest`, and `uv run python -m py_compile server.py`; resolve everything found.

Watch three disjoint loops fire: ruff catches the E402 import-order issue (the agent may briefly add duplicate imports — "this happens" — and re-run); **pytest catches Drill 1's commented-out `validate_sql_query`** — an agent with zero memory of Drill 1 un-comments it and restores the `SQLSecurityError` import; py_compile seals syntax.

**Checkpoint 2 (write it down):** one sentence on why `/clear` made the pytest catch *more* impressive, not less. *(A fresh agent with no memory of the sabotage still caught and fixed it — proof that validators carry your standards across context windows, which is what makes fresh agents safe.)*

## 3 · The full stack incl. the browser (20 min)

`/clear`. Reproduce the `# Validation` reusable prompt from frame t1200:
- **Backend:** ruff, `uv run pytest`, `uv run python -m py_compile server.py`
- **Frontend:** `cd app/client && bun tsc --noEmit`, `bun run build`
- **E2E (Playwright MCP):** open `localhost:5173`, screenshot before, run `select newest 7 products sort by price desc`, click Query, screenshot after, **read both images and confirm exactly 7 results.**

Run it. Then do Dan's ultimate spot-check yourself: open the after-screenshot, copy the generated query into the real app, confirm the identical 7 rows. Count your loops.

**Checkpoint 3:** you counted **six** (ruff, pytest, py_compile, tsc --noEmit, bun run build, Playwright e2e), and you can state what makes the "confirm 7 results" assertion trustworthy. *(`scripts/reset_db.sh` restored a known DB state first; without determinism the precise assertion means nothing.)*

## 4 · Templated loops — validation by default (20 min)

Run `/bug 111 adw111` with Dan's junk-data description: *tests write junk tables to the production SQLite DB; they should run against in-memory DBs instead.* **Do NOT implement yet.** Open the generated `specs/issue-111-adw-adw111-sdlc_planner-*.md` and verify three things:
1. a `## Validation Commands` section exists,
2. it includes reproduce-before / reproduce-after commands (table diffs, targeted pytest),
3. there is **no** e2e task — this is a backend-only bug, so the template's "IMPORTANT: if the bug affects the UI..." conditional correctly did NOT fire.

Then `/clear` and `/implement` the plan. Confirm all its validation commands pass and that `git status` shows no junk tables after `uv run pytest`.

**Checkpoint 4:** state what the `/bug` meta prompt guarantees about every plan it emits, and the exact condition that forces a new `.claude/commands/e2e/test_<name>.md` task. *(Every plan ends with a Validation Commands section; a new e2e file is forced whenever the bug affects UI or user interactions.)*

## 5 · The test node, out-loop-shaped (25 min)

Restore a clean state (commit or revert). Create a real issue on **your** repo — e.g. the debounce bug: *"disable the query input while a query is running, add a debounce."* Run the test node directly:

```
cd adws && uv run adw_test.py <issue-number>
```

Verify the full trail: `{adw_id}_`-prefixed issue comments, the 📊 **Test Run Summary** comment, a `test-issue-*` (or reused) branch, a commit with the sdlc-formatted message, a PR, and `agents/{adw_id}/` containing `test_runner/raw_output.jsonl` (plus `e2e_test_runner_*` dirs with `img/` screenshots if e2e ran).

**Checkpoint 5:** the run left a complete audit trail (prefixed comments, summary, commit, PR, per-agent prompts + `raw_output.jsonl`). If it failed, you can point to *where* the failure was reported, not guess at it.

## 6 · Read the trail like Dan (10 min)

From Drill 5's run, open `agents/{adw_id}/test_runner/prompts/test.txt` and `raw_output.jsonl`. Find the JSON array `/test` returned; confirm each entry carries an `execution_command` you could paste straight into a terminal. If anything failed, open the matching `test_resolver_iter*/` or `e2e_test_resolver_iter*/` directory and read the exact payload the resolver received.

**Checkpoint 6:** you diagnosed a real (or simulated) failure from saved artifacts alone — the on-camera skill that turned an out-loop FAILED status into "Anthropic API 500, infrastructure not product" in ninety seconds.

## Stretch drills (still zero hand-typing)

**S1 — New e2e spec.** Via Claude Code, create `.claude/commands/e2e/test_hide_button.md` modeled on `test_basic_query.md`: User Story → Test Steps (with `**Verify**` markers) → Success Criteria incl. a screenshot count. Execute via `/test_e2e` (pass an adw_id, agent name, the file); verify JSON output + screenshots under `agents/<id>/<agent>/img/hide_button/`.

**S2 — Break a loop on purpose.** Have Claude Code flip an assertion in `tests/core/test_sql_processor.py`, commit to a scratch branch, run `uv run adw_test.py <issue>`, and watch `resolve_failed_test` reproduce → fix → rerun. Then answer: what stopped the system from "fixing" it by deleting the test? *(Your review + the resolver's minimal-change instructions — rule of law is a human-enforced architecture decision, not a model behavior.)*

**S3 — Bound the loops.** Re-run Drill 5 with `--skip-e2e`; explain when that flag is correct (e2e too slow/flaky for this iteration) and what confidence you gave up. Then read `MAX_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS` (4) and `MAX_E2E_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS` (2) in `adw_test.py` and state why unbounded resolution would be worse than honest failure.

**S4 — Add a seventh loop.** Pick a validator the lesson didn't use (`uv run ruff format --check .`, a coverage threshold, `npm audit`) and thread it through all three altitudes: the `# Validation` reusable prompt, the `/bug` Plan Format defaults, and `test.md`'s sequence (with `test_name` / `test_purpose` / `execution_command`). One loop, three altitudes — that IS "templating your engineering."

**S5 — Answer the core question for YOUR codebase.** Write the validation menu for the repo you actually work on: for each class of work (bug / feature / chore / data), the exact commands that would prove it production-ready. Mark which are encodable today vs. which need architecture work first (the net-new advantage, inverted). This list is your next month of leverage.

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand; every edit flowed through a prompt (scratch prompt files allowed)
- [ ] Drill 1's ruff loop closed autonomously: sabotage introduced, flagged, resolved, re-validated green with no human edits
- [ ] Drill 2 performed **after** `/clear`, and you can articulate why the pytest catch proves validators enforce standards across fresh context windows
- [ ] Drill 3 stacked all six loops and produced before/after screenshots whose result you independently reproduced in the browser (7 rows)
- [ ] Drill 4's generated plan contains a Validation Commands section with reproduce-before/after commands and correctly omits the e2e task for a backend-only bug
- [ ] Drill 5 left a complete audit trail: prefixed issue comments, 📊 summary, commit, PR, and `agents/{adw_id}/` with per-agent prompts and `raw_output.jsonl`
- [ ] Oral check, no notes: the core validation question verbatim; request→validate→resolve; the six loops; the rule of law (and what to do when a test is genuinely wrong); `adw_test`'s retry bounds (4 unit / 2 e2e, e2e gated on green units, stop at first e2e failure); why `/test` returns JSON with `execution_command`

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **The single most common failure:** skipping `/clear` before Drill 2. If the agent still remembers Drill 1, the cross-context catch is fake and the whole lesson about validators-carry-standards evaporates. Enforce the clear.
- **Port conflict on boot** (Drill 0/5): a stale server holds `:5173`/the API port. Use the stop-then-start scripts; Dan hits exactly this at ~13:00. Teaches why runbooks state their starting state.
- **Determinism stall (Drill 3):** if a student skips `scripts/reset_db.sh`, "confirm 7 results" becomes noise and they wrongly distrust their strongest loop. The DB reset is not optional decoration — it's what makes the precise assertion an assertion.
- **One in-loop agent per repo (Drills 1–4):** this lesson does no worktrees — only one repo-mutating agent runs on your device at a time. That constraint is exactly what the out-loop architecture (Drill 5) removes; name it so students don't think it's a bug.
- **Honest failure is success (Drill 5/6):** if `adw_test` reports FAILED because of an Anthropic API 500, the system is *working* — it surfaced an infrastructure failure it genuinely can't resolve. Reward the accurate report; a loop that can't fail loudly can't be trusted to pass quietly.
- **Cost anxiety:** a full `adw_test.py` node spins several agents across fresh contexts — it is the most expensive drill. If budget is tight, S3's `--skip-e2e` is a legitimate way to see the node work for less; the pay-to-play conversation is itself part of the lesson.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** the review and document SDLC steps (TAC-6), full webhook/tunnel out-loop infrastructure (optional, TAC-4 territory), and multi-agent worktree parallelism. Deflect scope creep to keep the closed-loop primitive crisp.

# TAC-5 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)

TAC-5 ages well because it teaches a *mental model* — request → validate → resolve, stacked across disjoint failure classes — not a toolchain. The concept is dead-on for 2026; what moved is **packaging and enforcement**. The lesson wires every loop by hand inside prompt text and Python; current Claude Code can package those loops as Skills and enforce them as hooks. Six things shifted. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay. Dan pre-handles the cosmetic drift himself — the YOLO "Bypassing Permissions" banner and `think hard` IDK are period detail; *"we will be the ones prompting the errors"* is the timeless part.

---

## 1. Enforcement: closed loops in prompt text → hooks as rails  ⟵ the one config step short

**Course era:** the loop lives INSIDE the prompt (request/validate/resolve), and that remains the right mental model for judgment-bearing work. tac-5 already ships five lifecycle hooks — but uses them for logging and notification, not validation.
**Current:** Claude Code (mid-2026) can enforce loops mechanically — `PostToolUse` hooks that run ruff/pytest after every edit and feed failures straight back, `Stop` hooks that gate completion on a green suite. The rule of law stops being a prompt the agent *should* honor and becomes a rail it *cannot* cross. tac-5 is literally one config step short of this pattern.
**Book treatment:** overlay + "current practice" callout. Teach the prompt-level loop first (pedagogically perfect — you can watch the stdout land in context), then show the same non-negotiable moved into a hook. Split rule: **prompt-level loops for judgment, hook-level loops for non-negotiables.**
**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).

## 2. Packaging: reusable validation prompts → Agent Skills

**Course era:** the `# Validation` reusable prompt and the `.claude/commands` templates are the encoding — discovery, triggering, and composition all manual.
**Current:** Agent Skills (`SKILL.md` with frontmatter, on-demand discovery, composition, shareable across projects/teams) are the first-class form of exactly this. A "validate this repo" skill with embedded commands, e2e specs, and evidence rules is the modern shape of what this lesson builds by hand. Concept maps 1:1; packaging upgraded.
**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED — this is the named packaging gap for every prompt artifact in the chapter. Teach the templates first (no magic), then show the same workflow as a Skill.
**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).

## 3. Contracts: text-parsed JSON → structured outputs + Agent SDK

**Course era:** `adw_test.py` asks `/test` to "return ONLY JSON" and then `parse_json()`s markdown-wrapped output — period-accurate, instructive, and a little fragile.
**Current:** the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS) gives schema-validated structured outputs, session management, hooks, and subagents natively; `claude -p --output-format stream-json` (which `agent.py` already uses) grew into a full product surface. The CONTRACT idea — **code decides, agents judge** — is completely unchanged and is the transferable lesson.
**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the JSON-you-hope-parses has a grown-up form"), not a rewrite. The boundary where deterministic code owns retries and agents own judgment is the point; the SDK just makes that boundary type-safe.
**Overlay:** none needed.

## 4. Browser loop: Playwright MCP → wider computer-use menu

**Course era:** Playwright MCP as the browser validator (`--isolated --headless --viewport-size 1920,1080` in `.mcp.json`).
**Current:** Playwright MCP is still a standard, current choice and the config holds up — but browser validation now has more first-party routes: Claude's computer-use tooling, Chrome-DevTools MCP for performance/a11y loops, hosted browser sandboxes. The principle *"browser control is another tool for validating work"* aged perfectly; only the menu widened.
**Book treatment:** footnote listing the current options; keep Playwright as the worked example. No overlay.

## 5. Environment: Mac mini + cloudflared → managed out-loop

**Course era:** the PITER environment is a physical Mac mini running `trigger_webhook.py` behind a cloudflared tunnel.
**Current:** managed options now dominate the E in PITER — `claude-code-action` on GitHub Actions (issue/PR-triggered agents with the repo checkout as the environment), cloud sandboxes (E2B is literally teased in `.env.sample`), and Claude Code on the web for kicked-off background runs. The four PITER elements are invariant; the **E is now often rented**.
**Book treatment:** "current practice" box next to the webhook demo. The self-operating end state this builds toward is owned by later chapters (below), so keep this chapter's overlays testing-specific.
**Overlay candidate (deferred):** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity* (include_in_phase1: **no**; TAC-4/7/8 own that vision).

## 6. Models & UI: period detail, pre-handled

**Course era:** `agent.py` pins model strings (`'sonnet'|'opus'`), the demo shows course-era TUI, the YOLO "Bypassing Permissions" banner, and `think hard` as an IDK.
**Current:** newer model families and richer permission modes exist; none of it changes a single loop. Treat every screenshot as period detail.
**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected frames ("UI is period detail; the loop is identical today"). No overlay.

---

- **The core validation question** — "Given a unit of valuable work that's production ready, how would you, the engineer, test and validate this work?" — and its operational payoff: encode each answer into a command or tool call.
- **Request → validate → resolve** as the anatomy of a closed-loop prompt. More common now (slash commands, skills, CI prompts), not less.
- **Tests as the rule of law**, with the corollary (a wrong test gets fixed *as a test*, never routed around). If anything, more enforceable now via hooks.
- **Stacking confidence across disjoint failure classes** — the six loops each catch what the others structurally can't. Timeless.
- **The browser is a tool call** — drive UI, capture evidence, verify a precise expectation. Complexity-invariant.
- **Code decides, agents judge** — the JSON contract at the `/test` boundary. The SDK hardens it; the idea is the lesson.
- **Isolated SDLC nodes** — test as its own node with its own agents and context windows, independently improvable. This is *more* true with subagents.
- **Observability / adopt your agent's perspective** — per-agent saved prompts + `raw_output.jsonl`, ADW-ID-prefixed comments as a trace viewer. The reason an out-loop FAILED became a 90-second diagnosis.
- **Bounded loops** — 4 unit / 2 e2e retries, stop-on-nothing-resolved, e2e-stop-on-first-failure. The difference between self-correction and token-burning thrash.
- **The adoption gradient** — single prompt → in-loop closed loops → templated prompts → ADWs off your device → you, the test on top of the test. Beginner-safe and still exactly right.
